lede: Every clear Sentinel-2 look at Sri Lanka's larger river channels, turned into an estimated suspended-sediment signal: 879 one-kilometre river cells for 2024–2025, and 13 stations followed from 2019 to 2025. Switch seasons to watch the monsoons arrive; pick a station to see its year.
how: River channels were mapped from Sentinel-2 water frequency (strict MNDWI, NDVI and NIR test on the clearest scenes) combined with JRC Global Surface Water, keeping long, narrow water and dropping tanks, reservoirs, lagoons and the coast. For every scene with up to 70 % cloud, clear and spectrally pure river pixels (Sen2Cor scene classification; MNDWI, NDVI and SWIR checks) were converted to suspended particulate matter with the Nechad red-band algorithm and to turbidity with the Dogliotti (2015) red-band relation, using the coefficients published with ACOLITE. Each 1 km cell shows the median over all clear scenes in the selected season.
caveats: SPM is an uncalibrated red-band estimate (Nechad algorithm, published coefficients); no Sri Lankan field samples were used. Compare places and seasons, and read absolute g m⁻³ as indicative only.
Only channels wider than about 60 m are resolved, so upper catchments and small rivers are missing.
Cloud removes most southwest-monsoon views in the wet zone; seasonal medians there rest on fewer scenes (see the Scenes column).
Atmospheric correction is the land-oriented Sen2Cor product; some cells near the coast are lagoon or estuary reaches rather than rivers.
No rainfall or discharge data are included yet, so the rainfall-response and rating-curve checks are still to be run with gauge data.
repro: Code: sediment-rs/scripts/cog/10–16 in the Flood-Predict repository. It reads public Sentinel-2 Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (AWS Open Data) and JRC water data directly, so no Earth Engine account is needed. Coefficients and references are in docs/METHODS.md.
findings: October–November is the muddiest time of year. The second inter-monsoon gives the highest median at 10 of 13 stations, and this holds with the late-2025 flood removed. Across river cells seen in every season the median is 34 g m⁻³ in SIM against 24 in the southwest monsoon.

The dry-zone Mahaweli runs on a different clock. Its lower reaches are clearest in the southwest monsoon (median 28 g m⁻³), which is the dry season there, and most turbid in the first inter-monsoon and northeast monsoon (45–53 g m⁻³).

The Kalu carries more sediment than the Kelani. Lower-Kalu cells have a median of 62 g m⁻³ against 23 on the lower Kelani, and Putupaula reads higher than Colombo on 77 % of the clear days both were seen.

The lower Kalu is getting muddier. At Putupaula the median rose from 32 (2020–21) to 41 (2022–23) to 66 g m⁻³ (2024–25); the seasonal Kendall test gives about +18 % a year (FDR q = 0.004). Neighbouring rivers stay flat, so a processing change is unlikely. Sand mining and land-use change are candidates to check on the ground.

On the Kalu the sediment comes from upstream. Along the lower 54 km, red-band SPM rises from about 45 g m⁻³ near the mouth to 55–75 around Putupaula, then steps up to 100–200 beyond about 35 km toward Ellagawa in every season. The Kelani stays near 20 along its whole lower course. That points to sources in the Ellagawa–Ratnapura reaches, where gem dredging is documented; narrower channels there may add some bank contamination.

The late-November 2025 floods (Cyclone Ditwah) show as a sediment pulse. 490 river cells were seen during the floods, at a median of 5.4× their normal level (switch the layer to Flood 2025). The Kelani read 8–10× its normal level on 30 November (210 g m⁻³ at Colombo) and the lower Mahaweli 25–40× on 2 December. Values above about 500 g m⁻³ are beyond the red band's reliable range.

The southwest monsoon is nearly invisible in the wet zone. Wet-zone stations had 0–7 clear southwest-monsoon looks in seven years, against 44–47 on the dry-zone Mahaweli. Discharge-based rating curves are needed to fill this gap.

Method finding: the NIR band is not usable on these channels as processed. Red- and NIR-band estimates differ by 100–140 % because bright banks leak NIR into 20 m water pixels, so the map uses red-band SPM. The upstream-downstream check across the Mahaweli reservoirs is inconclusive (ratio 1.06, 95 % CI 0.77–1.70) because tributaries join between the two stations.
